P1.evidence: Second call in a live engagement; there is no opening or framing phase to score. The rep did open correctly for a follow-up by going straight to the homework — 'let me know how the conversation with your wife go last night' — which is the right move and got the real answer immediately.

P2.evidence: No baseline on a follow-up call, per spec. Worth noting positively that the rep clearly had the prior call's financial picture to hand and used it accurately: 'you told me yesterday that you got about 1600 left over most months. Yeah? And a card with some room on it.'

P3.evidence: Goals were established on the prior call. None are restated here, which is itself a weakness — with a spouse objection live, the prospect's own why is the strongest available lever and it was never brought back into the room.

P4.evidence: Not reachable on a follow-up objection call.

P5.evidence: Scored rather than marked N/A because the playbook explicitly requires returning to Phase 5 when hesitation surfaces, and this call is nothing but hesitation. It was never re-run. No two-year projection, no settle question, no 'why not', no line in the sand. The prospect handed over the exact material a consequence frame needs — a previous leg injury, a wife who fears he will re-injure it, and a season of work about to make him busier — and the rep answered each point administratively instead. Six calls into this batch, P5 has still not run once.

P6.evidence: The belief question was asked in weak form and immediately after the wife's refusal — 'But what are your thoughts on...' — drawing 'it's kind of steep... but it's something I want to do, but I won't be able to do it now.' That is a yes on desire and a no on capacity, which is not a clear yes, and the rep proceeded anyway. He kept moving forward through three separate refusals ('it wouldn't be a good foot right now', 'it's not going to work right now', 'That 3000, no, not right now') before relenting. The all-in question never ran. P6c is the specific failure: the script says do not move forward without a clear yes and return to Phase 5 if hesitation surfaces, and the rep did the opposite — he moved forward without one and reached for price structures instead.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted repeatedly and none of it landed. No payment collected; the financing application was declined; the previously taken deposit was refunded, so the engagement moved backwards. No Trevor onboarding, no agreement, no welcome sequence. The rep did handle the withdrawal well — offering the refund unprompted, stating 'I don't want to put you on account, man', taking ownership of a September reconnect and exchanging direct contact details — which preserves the relationship even though the phase scores zero.

objection_plays.detail: The defining objection of the call, and the play ran only in part. What ran: the responsibility move, well delivered — 'let's solve this piece together right now, and then it's just about you making the call for yourself. Because this is your health, man, yeah? That's a decision only you can really make.' The deposit-and-refund fallback also effectively ran, in reverse: a deposit had already been taken before the spouse conversation and was refunded when she said no, which is exactly the scripted mechanism operating as designed. What did not run is the move that mattered most here: 'Is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain?' The wife's objection was partly that he might re-injure his leg, which is a caring objection, and that question is built for it. Also missing: 'Money aside, do you personally feel this CAN get you to your goal?', the pre-emptive 'what obstacles might come up' (too late by this call), and the not-a-joint-decision-like-buying-a-house frame. The rep also learned only at 00:17:04 that the prospect is not currently working — 'Okay, now that makes more sense... so she's she has the power right now' — which means the entire play was being run against a misunderstanding of who actually holds the decision.

The best isolation move in this batch, and the only one delivered before any restructuring: 'you told me yesterday, nothing else is standing between you and doing this except the financial piece, right?' answered 'Yes.' The open-wallet question also ran in good form — 'So what number would actually feel comfortable to commit to monthly? No pressure. Just, you know, just, just tell me the real one' — producing an honest $200. The financial picture had been captured on the prior call and was recited accurately. Where it fails is what happened next: the script's purpose is to find a way to fund the stated price, and the rep instead moved down the price ladder, from $3,000 to instalments to external credit to a $1,000 self-paced product. The should-versus-how frame never appeared, and no attempt was made to establish when income resumes and what could be committed against it.

A textbook trigger arrived and nothing ran. The prospect deferred to September and gave the classic reason himself — 'once I start working, the season picks up... what if you get too busy or whatever, that's what she was concerned about too' — which is precisely the setup for 'Things never slow down. When does it actually become the right time?' None of the six moves was used: no never-another-busy-season, no compounding-cost, no 'what if all you had to do was show up and everything else was handled', no only-thing-you-can-control. The rep accepted the September date on first offer. Defensible on empathy grounds given the prospect has no income, but scored as a miss because the play exists and the trigger was unmistakable.

The doubt arrived second-hand through the spouse and had two parts: that he would start and not finish, and that he would re-injure his leg. The rep answered both with mechanism rather than with the play — the programme is built around your schedule and your current physical capacity, and 'if you would get injured for any reason... we always pause the subscription for the time that you need to get well.' That injury-pause commitment is a substantive answer and it is the strongest thing the rep said on this call. But no OE move ran: no certainty question, no pleasure-versus-pain, no bridge, no plane, no burned-before, no 'how will you know if you never actually try'. The doubts were addressed operationally and never resolved emotionally, which is why they were still live at the end.

SCRIPT GAP — the downsell. When the financing application was declined, the rep pivoted to a $1,000 six-month Primal University offer and screen-shared the platform for roughly five minutes. There is no scripted downsell path, no guidance on when it is appropriate, and no framing for it, so the rep improvised the positioning: 'if the finances are tight, this is at least something that gets you going... And you can build up towards the proper coaching.' The prospect declined it twice while making clear he wanted the real thing. Given a $6,000 list product, a $3,000 quoted price and a $1,000 alternative all appeared on one call, the principal needs to decide whether the ladder is sanctioned and where the floor is.

notes: The rep ran the two hardest moves in the book well — a clean isolation and an honest open-wallet question — and then had nowhere to take the answers, because the script's only response to 'I cannot afford it' is a financial picture that here produced a real ceiling of $200 a month. From there he walked the price down rather than working the timing, and OD, the one play built for 'not right now', never ran at all. Two things to escalate above coaching: this prospect is being quoted $3,000 rather than $6,000, and a credit application was submitted for a prospect with no current income whose household had already refused. The withdrawal itself was handled decently — unprompted refund, no pressure at the end, a real reconnect date.
